```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
ri <- function(x) knitr::inline_expr(x)
```

This article is for authors whose numbers end up in text that R builds: plot
titles and axis labels, console and log messages, the cells and captions of a
table. It assumes you know `vignette("values", package = "weft")` and
`vignette("wording", package = "weft")`. After it you will be able to put
weft markup in an R string, send the result to a plot, the console, cli or a
table, quote attribute values inside R strings, and say what happens when a
check in a string fails.

The chunks that draw a plot are not run when this article is built. The
others are run, and their output is shown as R gave it.

```{r}
library(weft)
```

## One call, several sinks

`weft()` takes a character vector of markup and resolves it. Every value,
governor, name and check in it is evaluated during the call, in the
environment that called it. The result holds what they printed, so changing a variable
afterwards changes nothing.

```{r}
k <- 3
area <- 0.00012
w <- weft("*Eucalyptus* at `r k`{.word} sites, `r area`{.sci} m^2^ each")
```

The object is a character vector with two forms of each element. Its content
is the **plain** text: Unicode, with no markup. Superscripts are Unicode
characters, emphasis loses its marks, and an entity such as `&times;` is its
character. The **markdown** text is kept in an attribute.

```{r}
as.character(w)
format(w, target = "markdown")
```

Printed by a chunk, the object writes its markdown, which the page then
renders:

```{r}
w
```

Each place a string can go takes the form it can show:

| Sink | Gets |
|---|---|
| a ggplot2 title, subtitle, caption or axis label | plain text |
| `cat()`, `paste()`, `sprintf("%s", )`, `message()`, `stop()`, `glue::glue()` | plain text |
| `print()` in a console | the console form: plain text with emphasis in italic and bold, where the console draws styles |
| `{.val {w}}` in a cli message | the console form; `{w}` gets plain text |
| a chunk that prints the object, inline R | markdown |
| a caption option R computes, `fig.cap = weft(...)` | markdown (`fig.alt` gets plain text) |
| `knitr::kable(caption = weft(...))` | plain text |

`format(w)` and `as.character(w)` are always plain, whatever the console can
draw. `format(w, target = "markdown")` gives the markdown and
`format(w, target = "ansi")` the console form.

In the prose of a document you do not need `weft()`: write the markup
directly. `weft()` is for text that no chunk option reaches.

## Plots

A ggplot2 label keeps the `weft` object and draws its plain text. Write the
title as you would write the sentence in prose:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
creek <- data.frame(
  site = c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower"),
  flow = c(0.0021, 0.0094, 0.0310),
  ntu = c(4.2, 7.9, 12.6)
)
n_high <- sum(creek$ntu > 10)

ggplot(creek, aes(flow, ntu)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(b) fmt_sci(b, target = "plain")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(b) fmt_num(b, target = "plain")) +
  labs(
    title = weft("Turbidity at `r nrow(creek)`{.word} sites"),
    subtitle = weft("[No site | One site | # sites]{n=n_high} read above the trigger"),
    x = weft("Flow (m^3^ s^-1^)"),
    y = "Turbidity (NTU)"
  )
```

The axis title draws as "Flow (m³ s⁻¹)", and the subtitle as "One site read
above the trigger". A plot draws no emphasis: `*Eucalyptus*` draws as
"Eucalyptus" in the plot's font. A formula in the markup keeps its TeX in the
plain text; for a formula in a plot, use plotmath.

**Scale labels.** A scale's `labels` argument takes a function of the breaks.
Every `fmt_*()` takes `target = "plain"`, so the tick labels print with the
same digits, minus sign and grouping as the numbers in the prose. Outside a
knit, `fmt_*()` and `weft()` read the same `_weft.yml`, so a script's tick
labels and its title agree.

```{r}
fmt_num(c(-1.5, 0, 2500), target = "plain")
fmt_sci(c(0.0021, 0.031), target = "plain")
```

**Captions.** In a knit with weft on, a caption written as a string is
resolved like prose. When R computes the caption, give it as a `weft()`
call. knitr gets the markdown for `fig-cap` and `tbl-cap`, and the plain text
for `fig-alt`:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-flow
#| fig-cap: !expr weft("Turbidity against flow at `r nrow(creek)`{.word} sites.")
#| fig-alt: !expr weft("Scatter plot of turbidity against flow at `r nrow(creek)`{.word} sites.")
ggplot(creek, aes(flow, ntu)) + geom_point()
```
````

In an R Markdown chunk header the same is `fig.cap = weft("...")`.

**PDF output.** The plain text uses Unicode superscripts and the minus sign
(U+2212). R's `pdf()` device cannot draw the minus sign or most of the
superscripts. For a plot with weft text that is saved as PDF, use
`cairo_pdf()` or a ragg device:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("flow.pdf", device = cairo_pdf)
ggsave("flow.png", device = ragg::agg_png)
```

In a knit, set the device for every chunk in the setup chunk, with
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "cairo_pdf")` for PDF output or
`dev = "ragg_png"` for HTML.

## The console and cli

`print()` writes each element on its own line. Where the console draws
styles, emphasis is italic, strong emphasis bold, and a failure marker bold
red. Nothing else differs, so with the styles removed the line is the plain
text. weft draws styles only where cli would draw its own: not under
`NO_COLOR`, not in a knit, not into a sink, and not on a terminal without
colour. This article is knit, so it shows the plain text:

```{r}
print(w)
```

To see the styles as escape codes, force colour:

```{r}
a <- withr::with_options(list(cli.num_colors = 256), format(w, target = "ansi"))
a
cli::ansi_strip(a)
```

In a cli message, `{.val {w}}` draws the console form, in cli's value colour
and without quotes. A plain `{w}` gets the plain text.

```{r}
cli::format_inline("Mapped {.val {w}}")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cli::cli_inform("{.val {w}}")      # emphasis drawn, in the value colour
cli::cli_inform("Plotted {w}")     # plain text
cli::cli_alert_success("Saved {.val {w}}")
```

Three things to know:

- Write `{.val {w}}` with nothing else inside the braces.
  `{.val text {w}}` pastes the value into the text and quotes the whole.
- Give the object to cli as a value, never as the template. A value is never
  read as a template, so braces in it (a TeX formula, say) stay text. As the
  template, `cli_inform(w)`, cli evaluates whatever it finds in braces. Write
  `cli_inform("{w}")`.
- Do not write weft markup into a cli template. cli reads `{.num}` as one of
  its own styles. Resolve the text with `weft()` first and pass the object.

## Tables

A column built with `weft()` holds plain text, so a data frame prints
readable cells. Build one element per row in a function, so each row reads
its own values:

```{r}
readings <- data.frame(
  site = c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower"),
  ntu = c(4.2, 7.9, 12.6),
  n = c(1, 3, 2)
)
note <- function(ntu, n) {
  weft("`ntu`{.num} NTU, [**high** | normal]{if='ntu > 10'}, from [one sample | # samples]{n=n}")
}
readings$note <- do.call(c, Map(note, readings$ntu, readings$n))
readings
```

`c()` of `weft` objects keeps both forms. For a table rendered as markdown,
give `kable()` the markdown of the column, so the emphasis is drawn. A
`weft()` caption reaches `kable()` as plain text:

```{r}
shown <- readings[c("site", "note")]
shown$note <- format(readings$note, target = "markdown")
knitr::kable(shown, caption = weft("Turbidity at `r nrow(readings)`{.word} sites"))
```

## Messages and logs

`message()`, `warning()` and `stop()` paste their arguments, so they get the
plain text:

```{r}
n_files <- 4
message(weft("Read `n_files`{.word} files."))
```

A helper that wraps `weft()` must pass its caller's environment on, or the
markup reads the helper's own variables:

```{r}
log_line <- function(text) message(weft(text, .envir = parent.frame()))
n_rows <- 1250
log_line("Kept `n_rows`{.num} rows.")
```

To write a log file, write the plain text, with `writeLines(format(w), con)`
or `cat()`. Do not write `format(w, target = "ansi")` to a file: its form
depends on the console that wrote it.

In a chunk with `results = "asis"`, `cat()` writes the plain text, and so
does an explicit `print()`. To write markdown from a loop, write
`cat(format(w, target = "markdown"), "\n\n")`. Only an object the chunk
prints at its top level is written as markdown by knitr.

## Quoting inside R strings

An attribute value goes in double quotes, in single quotes, or in none when
it is one word, as in prose. In R code the choice matters, because the
markup sits inside an R string. Give the values the quote the R string does
not use:

```{r}
tier <- "sev"
as.character(weft("[severe | mild]{if='tier == \"sev\"'}"))
as.character(weft('[severe | mild]{if="tier == \'sev\'"}'))
```

Both calls give weft the same block. In the first, the R string is in double
quotes, the value in single quotes, and the R string inside the value in
escaped double quotes, which R reads as plain `"` before weft sees the text.

A value of one word, such as a name, needs no quotes: `{n=n_high}`,
`{digits=2}`.

Inside a quoted value weft reads four escapes: `\"`, `\'`, `\|` and `\ `
(backslash, space). The last is how a value starts with a space, as the
`last` of `.and` may need. Any other backslash in a value is an error. In an
ordinary R string a backslash is itself written `\\`, so weft's `\ ` is
`\\ ` in the R source:

```{r}
sites <- c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower")
as.character(weft("`sites`{.and last='\\ plus '}"))
```

A raw string (R 4.0 and later) holds the text as written: quotes of both
kinds need no R escape, and weft's backslash is written once:

```{verbatim, lang = "r"}
weft(r"([severe | mild]{if='tier == "sev"'})")
weft(r"(`sites`{.and last="\ plus "})")
```

A raw string `r"(...)"` ends at the first `)"`. A value that ends in `)`
then takes single quotes (`{if='isTRUE(x)'}`), or the raw string takes other
brackets or dashes: `r"[...]"`, `r"---(...)---"`.

## Bare names read R

A name in a code span with a class, `` `ntu`{.num} ``, reads R where the
`weft()` call runs: it prints what `` `r ri("ntu")`{.num} `` would print, with
every formatter, units and the dictionary included. Names in a governor,
such as `{n=n}`, are R code in the same place.

The name is looked up in `.envir` (by default the caller) and its enclosing
environments, as far as the global environment, and no further. A name is
never read from base R, a package or a dataset. In a loop, each call reads
the names as they stand at that call:

```{r}
depth <- c(Upper = 0.42, Lower = 1.37)
titles <- lapply(names(depth), function(site) {
  d <- depth[[site]]
  weft("Depth at `site`{.val}: `d`{.num digits=2} m")
})
print(do.call(c, titles))
```

A name that is not bound there, or that is bound to a function, is a "no
value" failure. Nothing is left for a Pandoc filter, because the text goes
to plots and consoles where none runs:

```{r pi-name, error = TRUE}
weft("A circle's area is `pi`{.num} r^2^.")
```

`` `r ri("pi")`{.num} `` reads base R's `pi`. To use a name from a package,
bind it first: `n <- pkg::n`.

From a Python chunk in a knitr document, `weft_str()` in the weft Python
module calls `weft()` and returns the markdown. There a named value is
Python's, published with `put()`; see
`vignette("languages", package = "weft")`.

## When something fails

**Outside a knit**, in a script or at the console, the first failure stops
at once. Its class says what failed: `weft_claim_failed`, `weft_no_value`,
`weft_value_error` or `weft_construct_error`. The message begins
`weft: a weft() string:`. Draft mode has no effect. A warning, such as a
value printed as zero, is signalled and the object is returned.

The same holds in a knit where `weft_setup()` was not called, as in this
article. There the message names the chunk:

```{r peak, error = TRUE}
peak <- 61
weft("The peak was `r claim(peak, . < 50)`{.num} NTU.")
```

A script can catch a failure by its class:

```{r catch-class}
title <- tryCatch(
  weft("The peak was `r claim(peak, . < 50)`{.num} NTU."),
  weft_claim_failed = function(e) {
    message("Check the peak: ", conditionMessage(e))
    weft("The peak was above the limit.")
  }
)
```

**In a knit with weft on**, a failure in a `weft()` string is collected as
one in a paragraph is. The knit goes on, and the render fails at the end with
every failure listed, each located by the chunk that holds the call (or the
line, for inline R). A construct error stops the render at once, except in
draft mode. In draft mode the render finishes and the text carries a marker
where the value would be, in a plot title as in prose:

```text
The peak was 61<<weft: failed claim, chunk fig-peak>> NTU.
```

Outside a knit, `weft()` reads the `_weft.yml` of the project the working
directory is in: the nearest folder upward that holds `_weft.yml`, else
`_quarto.yml`, else the working directory itself. It reads the file once per
session, and again when it changes, so a call in a loop costs little. A
`_weft.yml` with an error is a `weft_config_error`.

## Scripts are linted

The lints, the commit gate, `arms()` and `checks()` read the literal strings
given to `weft()`, in the R chunks of a document and in the project's `.R`
files. A typed number in `weft("We found 12 sites")` in `R/plots.R` is a
`numeral` finding, as it would be in prose, and a construct error there fails
a commit. Write the number as a value:
``weft("We found `n_sites`{.word} sites")``.

Only a literal is read: a string, a raw string, or the literal elements of a
`c()`. A computed argument, such as `weft(paste0(...))` or `weft(txt)`, is
skipped. Keep the markup literal and let the names inside it carry the data.
Files under `tests/` are not read unless `scripts_skip` says otherwise. The
details are in the "Scripts" section of
`vignette("lints", package = "weft")`.

Markup in an R string that never reaches `weft()` prints as typed. In a
document's chunks the `string-markup` lint finds such a string.
